entry.title: The radish that looks like a firecracker

link.title: The radish that looks like a firecracker

entry.content:
Pulled the last of the watermelon radishes this week and they are exactly as dramatic as I hoped. Plain tan on the outside, then you slice one open and there’s that hot-pink ring staring back at you. I’ve been eating them with salt and butter and nothing else.

They’re mild this time of year — the cold nights kept them from getting peppery. Slice them thin and they’re almost sweet. Slice them thick and there’s just a little bite at the end. Either way, the color is the whole point. Put them on a plate and people ask questions.

"The cold nights kept them from getting peppery. Thin-sliced, they're almost sweet."

Edgie · May 2026

I’ve got about four flats left, so this Saturday will likely be the last of them until fall. Sugar snap peas are right behind them — the vines hit the top wire two days ago and the first pods are just starting to swell. Those should be at the stall by late May.

See you Saturday at stall #14.

entry.title: Asparagus: two weeks, then it’s gone

link.title: Asparagus: two weeks, then it’s gone

entry.content:
The asparagus bed is up. Three years of waiting — I planted crowns in spring of 2023, left them alone in 2024, left them mostly alone in 2025, and now here we are. Worth every year of it.

Asparagus has the shortest window of anything I grow. Once the soil warms past 50°, the spears come up faster than you can harvest them, and then the plant wants to fern out and put its energy into next year. You get maybe two good weeks of picking before you have to let it go. We’re in week one right now.

This Saturday I’ll have pencil-thin spears — the kind that don’t need peeling, just snap off the woody end and you’re done. Roast them at high heat with olive oil and salt for ten minutes. That’s all they need.

First-come. I won’t have more than a few bundles.

entry.title: The market is back
entry.content:
First Saturday of the season. The St. Paul Farmers’ Market opens rain or shine and this year it opened in 38 degrees and a wind that came straight off the river. Sold out of chard by 9am anyway.

Spring at a market garden is a strange season. Everything is small and cold-weather and most people are still thinking about soup. But that’s exactly when the best stuff is here — the greens are sweet from the frost, the roots are dense, and nothing has had time to get tired or bitter. Cold-weather vegetables taste like they’re trying to prove something.

This year I’m starting with butterhead lettuce, rainbow chard, spring garlic, and the first of the radishes. Watermelon radishes are still sizing up — give them another two weeks. Asparagus crowns went in their third season, so if the math works out, we’ll have those in late April.

Come find us at stall #14, east end. I’ll be the one in the apron that used to be green.
